faq.q: What kind of laser cuts metal?
faq.a: Most metal cutters use fibre lasers, where light is amplified inside a special glass fibre, or carbon dioxide gas lasers. Industrial machines typically have powers from one to tens of kilowatts.

faq.q: Why does focusing make the laser so powerful?
faq.a: Focusing does not add energy, it concentrates it. A few kilowatts squeezed into a spot a tenth of a millimetre wide gives a power density millions of times stronger than sunlight, enough to melt steel instantly.
asks: How hot does a laser cutter get?

faq.q: Why does a laser cutter use gas?
faq.a: The assist gas blows molten metal out of the cut so it does not re-weld, and protects the lens. Nitrogen stops the edge oxidising; oxygen reacts with hot steel, adding heat for faster cutting of thick plate.
Laser cutters typically cut to about a tenth of a millimetre or better, with a very narrow cut, called the kerf, often 0.1 to 0.3 millimetres wide, so little metal is wasted.
The invisible beam can blind instantly and burn skin, so industrial laser cutters are fully enclosed with special viewing windows, and fumes are extracted. Operators never look into the beam.

facts: The first working laser was built by Theodore Maiman in 1960.
A laser cut, called the kerf, is typically only about 0.1 to 0.3 mm wide.
